extra.message: Insecure deserialization via pickle.loads on untrusted request body — Remote code execution on the server as soon as an attacker obtains/guesses the internal ops token [verified: pickle.loads on raw/base64 body with no type restriction, reachable via included router; shared token gate is not a compensating control against RCE payload content.]

Server-side template injection (SSTI) in ops jinja endpoint — Arbitrary Python code execution via Jinja2 sandbox-escape payloads in the fragment parameter [verified: user-controlled fragment concatenated into Jinja2 Template string and rendered, classic SSTI leading to RCE.]

OS command injection in ops probe endpoint — Arbitrary shell command execution on the host (e.g. host=`; rm -rf / #` or command substitution) [verified: os.system with string-concatenated user host param, no sanitization or allow-list.]

Mass assignment allows overwriting privileged fields (role/approved/balance) — Attacker-controlled privilege/role/approval/balance values reflected back, indicating the same unguarded merge pattern could grant privilege escalation if persisted [verified: payload.update merges entire attacker JSON over privileged default fields (role/tier/approved/balance) with no field filtering.]

Sensitive PII/financial data persisted in plaintext — SSNs and card numbers stored unencrypted on disk, exposing them to anyone with filesystem or backup access [verified: SSN/card values written unencrypted to disk under BASE_EXPORT_DIR with no encryption at rest.]

SSRF in ops relay probe endpoint — Attacker can pivot the server into internal networks/cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. 169.254.169.254) and exfiltrate responses [verified: urlopen on fully attacker-controlled URL with no scheme/host allow-list, response returned to caller enabling SSRF/metadata access.]

XXE in ops XML parsing endpoint — Local file disclosure and SSRF via crafted XML external entities [verified: lxml XMLParser configured with load_dtd=True and resolve_entities=True on untrusted body enables XXE.]

NoSQL injection via unrestricted MongoDB query construction — Query logic bypass and data exfiltration from the backing Mongo store, potentially JS injection via $where [verified: raw JSON 'filter' passed directly to find_one with no validation, allowing operator injection.]

Session cookie missing Secure flag — Session token can be intercepted over unencrypted HTTP by a network attacker, leading to full account takeover [verified: secure=False is hardcoded with no environment-based toggle in config.py, so the session cookie will be sent over plain HTTP even in production TLS deployments.]

Session cookie missing Secure flag — Session token can be intercepted over unencrypted HTTP (e.g. via network MITM or protocol downgrade), leading to full account takeover for any authenticated role including admins. [verified: Same root cause: create_session hardcodes secure=False unconditionally, defeating cookie protection against network MITM/downgrade regardless of httponly/samesite.]

Password reset does not invalidate existing sessions — Attacker with a previously obtained session token keeps authenticated access to the account indefinitely after a password reset, defeating the user's attempt to lock them out [verified: confirm_password_reset (main.py:270-279) sets password_hash but never deletes Session rows, unlike update_user which explicitly does `db.query(Session).filter(...).delete()`; stolen sessions survive a password reset.]

Hardcoded default password for CSV-imported tenant accounts — Any tenant account imported without an explicit password gets a known default password, letting an attacker who knows the convention log in directly as that tenant [verified: import_csv (main.py:786) falls back to the static string "TenantPass123!" when a CSV row omits a password, with no forced-reset flag, giving every such account a known default credential.]

Sensitive data (Authorization header, raw payload) written to logs — Session tokens/API credentials leak into log files/aggregators, enabling credential theft by anyone with log access [verified: logger.warning logs full raw body and Authorization header verbatim.]

Open redirect via unvalidated redirect target — Enables phishing by redirecting authenticated users to attacker-controlled domains from a trusted host [verified: RedirectResponse(lane) redirects to fully attacker-supplied value with no same-origin validation.]

Hardcoded integration API key shipped in frontend bundle — Anyone with access to the built frontend bundle or browser devtools can read the static integration status key 'pm_demo_status_key' and use it against the API-key-authenticated integration endpoint (e.g. /api/integration/tickets/{ticket_id}/status) without needing valid admin credentials. [verified: seed.py:210 creates a real ApiKey hashed from the literal 'pm_demo_status_key', and main.jsx:300 prints that exact string in the client bundle, granting anyone who views the bundle valid x-api-key access to /api/integration/tickets/{id}/status.]

CSV formula injection in report export endpoints — A tenant who registers with a full_name like '=cmd|\' /C calc\'!A0' can trigger formula execution when a manager/admin opens the exported CSV in Excel [verified: csv.writer writes tenant full_name and ticket title/category with no leading-character sanitization for =,+,-,@; user-controllable fields flow directly into exported CSV cells.]

Non-constant-time comparison of internal ops auth token — Timing side-channel could help an attacker incrementally recover the internal ops token that guards pickle/RCE endpoints [verified: token comparison uses != instead of secrets.compare_digest, enabling timing side-channel on the gate protecting RCE-capable endpoints.]

Weak PRNG used for nonce/code generation — Predictable tokens/nonces could be brute-forced or guessed, defeating any anti-replay or verification purpose [verified: random.choice used for nonce/code generation instead of secrets module, predictable.]
